title: ALTER TABLE & Schema Evolution
description: Modify existing tables, rename columns, change data types, and manage table locks during migrations.

data.text: As applications grow, tables must adapt. **`ALTER TABLE`** adds, drops, or modifies columns and constraints. Understanding the lock level acquired by `ALTER TABLE` is critical to avoiding application outages during deployments.

data.title: Safe ALTER TABLE Operations in PostgreSQL 11+
data.content: Adding columns with default values in modern PostgreSQL does not rewrite the table.

data.text: The Lock Level Is the Whole Story

In production, the danger with `ALTER TABLE` is rarely correctness — it is the lock it takes. Most `ALTER TABLE` variants take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, which blocks **reads as well as writes**, and the lock is held until the transaction commits. If the migration also does a long data backfill, every query on that table queues behind it.

rows: e.g. `DEFAULT random()` requires a rewrite — add, then backfill.
Metadata only; disk space reclaimed later.
Rewrites the whole table unless the cast is binary-coercible (e.g. `varchar(50)`→`text`).
Scans the table to verify, but no rewrite once validated.
Skips the validation scan; validate later with a `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock.
Runs concurrently with reads and writes.
Does not block writes; cannot run inside a transaction.

data.title: Adding a Column With a Default, Safely

items.text: Set a short lock timeout so the migration fails fast instead of queuing behind a long query
Add the column as NULLable with no default

items.hint: Avoid one huge UPDATE; keeps bloat and lock time low

items.text: Add the default for new rows
Add `NOT NULL` — or, on PG 12+, the constraint is validated without a rewrite
items.hint: Use `NOT VALID` + `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` if you need to avoid the scan lock

data.title: Zero-Downtime Column Addition and Backfill
data.content: Run the backfill outside the DDL transaction, in batches.

data.caption: Expand/contract: the pattern that keeps deploys backwards compatible
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Old code + old schema] --> B[Expand: add new nullable column]
    B --> C[Deploy code that writes BOTH columns]
    C --> D[Backfill old rows]
    D --> E[Switch reads to the new column]
    E --> F[Contract: drop old column in a later release]
    F --> G[New code + new schema]

data.text: The key insight is that the schema change is split across **two deployments**. Deploying the schema first (expand) means the running old code still works. Dropping in a later release (contract) means a rollback is still possible until you are confident.

data.title: Never Rename in Place During a Deploy
data.text: A rename is instant for the database but instantly breaks any app server running the previous version. Expand/contract — add the new name, dual-write, migrate readers, drop the old name — avoids the outage.

items.question: Why does `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT false` not rewrite the table?
items.answer: Since PostgreSQL 11, a non-volatile default is stored as a single catalog entry that applies to existing rows on read, so only new rows ever materialise the value.

items.question: How do I add a `NOT NULL` constraint without a long lock?
items.answer: Add it as a `CHECK` constraint with `NOT VALID`, then run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` (which takes only a `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock), and finally `ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL`, which can use the proven check constraint instead of rescanning.

items.question: Can `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` run in a migration transaction?
items.answer: No. It must be its own statement outside a transaction block. If it fails it can leave an invalid index you must drop and recreate.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Adding a column with a constant default in PostgreSQL 11+ is fast and does not rewrite the heap.
Changing column types or dropping columns should be done using Expand-and-Contract patterns.
